      <title>Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/18/lagos-hypemen-redefining-afrobeats-music-afrohype</link>
      <description><p>Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds</p><p>For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.</p><p>His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/18/lagos-hypemen-redefining-afrobeats-music-afrohype">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next </p><p>A dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.</p><p>Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors peered down on the scene.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/18/4000-people-minding-our-own-business-four-decades-on-falklands-again-face-a-hostile-argentina">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>EPA quietly backtracks on claims US has phased out toxic Pfas compounds</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/18/epa-pfas-compounds-toxins</link>
      <description><p>Agency changes wording on website as Texas-based firm continues manufacture of plastic container barriers</p><p>The Environmental Protection Agency has quietly backtracked on a claim that the US has phased out two of the most dangerous Pfas compounds – Pfoa and Pfos.</p><p>The EPA has found that <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/06/21/2022-13158/lifetime-drinking-water-health-advisories-for-four-perfluoroalkyl-substances?utm_source=chatgpt.com">virtually no level of exposure</a> to either in drinking water is safe, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer <a href="https://www.iarc.who.int/news-events/iarc-monographs-volume-135-perfluorooctanoic-acid-pfoa-and-perfluorooctanesulfonic-acid-pfos/">classifies Pfoa </a>as “carcinogenic to humans” and Pfos as “possibly carcinogenic”. Still, the EPA is allowing Houston-based Inhance to produce containers from which Pfoa <a href="https://pubs.acs.org/estlcu/article-abstract/10/4/350/345648/Directly-Fluorinated-Containers-as-a-Source-of?redirectedFrom=fulltext">has been found</a> to leach at high levels into the containers’ contents. The company makes up to 200m barriers annually for plastic containers used across the US economy.</p><p>This article was amended on 18 October 2026 to correct Patricia van Ee’s title, and the story previously stated that Inhance manufactures plastic containers. They make the containers’ barriers.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/18/epa-pfas-compounds-toxins">Continue reading...</a></description>
